content:
A common question asks when the 27 books of the New Testament were collected, and by whom. A common answer names a church council, or an emperor. The surviving lists tell a longer story.

Seven facts follow, from the first collection to the councils of North Africa. They draw on the lists themselves, and on a history of the canon written in 1877 that sets out what each writer and council said, page by page.

Marcion brought a collection to Rome in 144, by Davidson's reckoning. It held ten letters of Paul and an altered form of Luke.[1]

Other collections of Paul's letters and of gospels circulated before him, so the earliest list of a church is not the earliest collection of books. It is the earliest list that survives with a clear owner.

Davidson describes a New Testament of "the gospel" and "the apostle". The first held the four gospels. The second held Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, 1 Peter, 1 John and the Revelation.[2]

Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian each added an appendix of further books, such as the Shepherd of Hermas, Hebrews, Jude, Barnabas and the Apocalypse of Peter. Davidson's summary is that "These three fathers did not fix the canon absolutely."[3]

The fragment names the four gospels, Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, Jude, two letters of John and the Apocalypse. It allows the Shepherd of Hermas to be read, and it rejects letters "to the Laodiceans" and "to the Alexandrians" as forged in Paul's name.[4]

Davidson dated it about 170 and placed it in Rome. That was the standard view until the 1970s. Some scholars have since argued for the fourth century, and others still prefer the second, so the date is contested.

Origen had three classes: the acknowledged books, the mixed, and those not authentic. Eusebius, in the early fourth century, sorted books into the recognised, the disputed and the heretical.[5]

His disputed class held James, 2 Peter, Jude, and 2 and 3 John. A historian who names a book as disputed in AD 325 gives evidence that no list was closed.

A list of the African church, copied in the Clermont manuscript, adds Barnabas in the place of Hebrews, and the Shepherd of Hermas, the Acts of Paul and the Revelation of Peter, after the main books.[6]

The Syriac Peshito lacks 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and the Apocalypse. Davidson put it in the early third century. A later date, in the early fifth, is now usual.[7]

Athanasius of Alexandria wrote the list in his Easter letter of 367. Davidson dates the letter to 365. Later work gives 367, and the later date is the one to quote.[8]

The Greek church was not of one mind even then. The Council of Laodicea lists in its 60th canon books without the Apocalypse, though Davidson, following an earlier scholar, held that canon to be later than the council. Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nazianzus and Amphilochius also omit the Apocalypse.

The African councils of Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 and 419 fixed the New Testament as we have it, and Carthage in 419 counts fourteen letters of Paul. The Eastern church adopted the Apostolic canons at the Trullan council of 692.[9]

Davidson wrote that "No definite principles guided the course of its formation, or fixed its present state."[10] That is a nineteenth-century judgment. The lists themselves support a narrower statement: no single council, and no emperor, chose the 27 books for every church.

The bottom line

Each list was a record of what one writer or one region read. The 27 books were gathered by use and argument over some three centuries, and councils later confirmed lists for their own churches.[11]

A person who asks which New Testament the Quran meant needs to read the lists, and the lists differ.

Notes

  1. Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible: Its Formation, History, and Fluctuations (New York: Peter Eckler, 1877), p. 58.
  2. Davidson, Canon, pp. 71 to 72.
  3. Davidson, Canon, pp. 71 to 72.
  4. Davidson, Canon, pp. 72 to 73. On the date: Albert C. Sundberg, "Canon Muratori: A Fourth-Century List", Harvard Theological Review 66 (1973), pp. 1 to 41; Geoffrey Mark Hahneman, The Muratorian Fragment and the Development of the Canon (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1992).
  5. Davidson, Canon, pp. 75 to 77. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.25.
  6. Davidson, Canon, pp. 74 to 75.
  7. Davidson, Canon, p. 75; Bruce M. Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament: Its Origin, Development, and Significance (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1987).
  8. Davidson, Canon, pp. 88 to 92; the dating of the letter follows Metzger, Canon of the New Testament.
  9. Davidson, Canon, pp. 96 to 101, 103 and 107.
  10. Davidson, Canon, pp. 96 to 101, 103 and 107.
  11. Lee Martin McDonald, The Biblical Canon: Its Origin, Transmission, and Authority, 3rd ed. (Peabody: Hendrickson, 2007); F. F. Bruce, The Canon of Scripture (Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press, 1988).
